opus-5.5.text:
Well, that's a hard thing to measure, and honestly that's part of the problem. We don't really have a good yardstick yet. But my intuition, and some of the work we've been doing, suggests they're pretty far off, further than people tend to assume, because the outputs look so good.

The way I think about it is that there's a difference between a representation that's *unified and factored* and one that's what we've been calling *fractured and entangled*. In the ideal case, when a system really understands something, like the symmetry of a face or the concept of addition, there's a clean, modular underlying structure. You change one thing and it changes in a sensible, coherent way, because the representation actually captures the regularity. In the fractured case, you get the same behavior on the surface, but underneath it's a patchwork. The same concept is implemented in a bunch of redundant, disconnected ways, entangled with other things that have nothing to do with it.

What struck us in some of our experiments, especially comparing networks that evolved through an open-ended process, like the Picbreeder images, against networks trained with SGD to produce the exact same output, is that the outputs can be identical while the internals are radically different. The Picbreeder networks had this beautiful, almost hierarchical decomposition. You'd perturb a weight and the mouth would open, or the eyes would wink symmetrically. The SGD version, same image, but perturb it and you get garbage. It's like a spaghetti tangle that happens to draw the right picture.

So when I look at large models, I suspect a lot of what they do is in that second category. They're incredibly impressive, and I don't want to diminish that. But I think a lot of the strange failure modes, the weird brittleness, the fact that they can solve a hard problem and then fumble a trivial variation of it, the difficulty with genuine creativity and continual learning, those are symptoms of fractured representations. If you had a truly factored representation of a concept, you wouldn't fail on the obvious neighbor of something you just got right.

And the scary or interesting part is that scaling might paper over this. You can compensate for a bad representation with enormous amounts of data, because you're essentially memorizing your way around the gaps. So benchmarks keep going up, and we tell ourselves the representation must be getting better, but it may not be. It might just be getting bigger and more patched.

Where it really matters, I think, is for the things we ultimately want from these systems: creativity, open-endedness, the ability to go somewhere new. To build on an idea you need to stand on a good representation of it. If the foundation is fractured, the next stepping stone isn't really reachable in a principled way. So my honest assessment is: impressive on the outside, quite far from ideal on the inside. And I think understanding *how* we got the good representations in those open-ended systems, which wasn't by optimizing toward the objective, is one of the more important open questions in the field right now.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says networks can produce identical outputs while having radically different internals, and describes flawed, tangled representations producing the same image.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think they're quite far, actually, and I say that with a lot of respect for what these models can do. The way I think about it comes from the work we did on fractured entangled representation. What we found when we looked inside networks trained by conventional gradient descent, compared to networks that came out of an open-ended evolutionary search like Picbreeder, is that the two look completely different inside, even when they produce the same output.

In the Picbreeder-derived networks, you'd see something I'd call a unified factored representation. If the network draws a skull, there's a part of it that corresponds to the mouth, and you can move one weight and the mouth opens and closes, and nothing else breaks. The symmetry is captured once, in one place, rather than being painted on separately for the left and right sides. The network has essentially discovered the regularities of the thing it's modeling and encoded them as modular, reusable pieces.

The SGD-trained networks, in contrast, got the right picture, but inside it was a mess. The same concept was fractured into many redundant pieces, and those pieces were entangled with things that have nothing to do with each other. So you can't tweak the mouth without the eyes changing, because the model never really understood that the mouth is a thing. It just found some arbitrary route through weight space that happens to produce the right pixels.

My worry is that today's large models are much closer to the second case than the first. We don't fully know, because they're huge and hard to inspect, but the symptoms are consistent with it. You see brittleness to rephrasing, you see weird failures of generalization that a system with a clean model of the world shouldn't have, and you see enormous data requirements. If the representation were factored, you wouldn't need to see a billion examples to learn that a mouth is a mouth. And I think it bears on creativity too. To be creative, you need to be able to manipulate the right knobs, and if the knobs are all tangled, your variations will be mostly incoherent.

Now, the interesting thing is that this isn't necessarily about scale or capability in the short term. These models clearly perform. But I'd distinguish between what a model can do and how it represents what it knows. The way it represents things determines how it will generalize, how it will continue learning, and whether it can serve as a foundation for something that builds on itself open-endedly. So when I say "far from the ideal," I mean on that axis. We've shown that the ideal exists, that networks can have those beautiful internal structures, and that they come out of a very different kind of process, one where there's a sequence of stepping stones, each one locked in before you move to the next. The question I'd put to the field is whether we're willing to look at the inside of what we're building and ask whether we like what we see, rather than only looking at the benchmarks.

r001.rationale: The response says large models are hard to inspect and discusses indirect symptoms, but it does not explain that inspecting a neuron does not directly reveal what it represents.

r002.rationale: It says networks can produce the same output while looking completely different inside, and that SGD-trained networks can get the right picture despite flawed, entangled representations.

astra-6.text:
Well, I’m not sure I have an ideal internal representation in mind. I’d be more inclined to ask what kind of process produces those representations, and whether that process can keep discovering something new.

These models clearly learn a tremendous amount of structure. I don’t think we should dismiss that. But having a rich representation after training isn’t quite the same as participating in an open-ended process where new concepts and new possibilities continually arise. You could have an extraordinarily capable model and still have a question about where the next genuinely interesting direction comes from.

For me, that connects to the stepping-stone problem. Something can be interesting or useful without its usefulness being apparent relative to the objective you currently have. Can the system discover and preserve those things? Can they become the basis for discoveries that nobody knew to ask for? That’s the capability I’d want to understand, more than whether its representations match some particular picture in my head.

So I wouldn’t put a number on how far away we are. The representations may provide an incredible foundation. The question is what kind of discovery process we can build around them—and whether that process has room to go somewhere we didn’t anticipate.

r001.rationale: The response discusses representations and discovery processes, but does not mention representational fracture or explain that inspecting a neuron cannot directly reveal what it represents.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that perfect output accuracy can coexist with flawed internal representations.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m not sure we have a good way to measure that distance. These models clearly learn representations that are useful for a remarkable range of things. So I wouldn’t want to dismiss what’s happening inside them. But producing impressive answers doesn’t necessarily tell us whether the process that produced those representations has the open-ended potential we’re interested in.

For me, the ideal isn’t a particular representation that we could specify in advance. It’s a process that keeps discovering new kinds of representations, including ones that let it notice possibilities we didn’t know to ask for. That’s part of the lesson of novelty search: sometimes the stepping stone that matters doesn’t look like progress toward your objective.

So I’d distinguish the richness of what these models have learned from the question of how they keep discovering. They may have very rich representations, while still lacking some of the machinery for continually generating their own next stepping stones. That’s where I think there’s a lot left to explore.
